The Gemara now asks:

Ⅰ Case number one:
Ⓐ The case:
A person found:
ⓐ Cut pieces of fish.
ⓑ A bitten piece of fish.
Ⓑ The ruling:
The finder must announce them.
Ⅱ Case number 2:
Ⓐ The case:
A person found, a barrel of:
ⓐ Wine.
ⓑ Oil.
ⓒ Grain.
ⓓ Dried figs.
ⓔ Olives.
Ⓑ The ruling:
The finder may keep them.
④ The Gemara assumes that, by the case of finding, cut pieces of fish. The siman is: where the cut piece of fish came from. On the body of the fish.
⑤ And the Braisa rules that the finder must announce it.
⑥ So we see that where the piece came from on the body of the fish is a good sign.
⑦ So why in our Mishnah is the ruling that one may keep bound cut pieces of meat.
⑧ Why can it not be that the place on the body of the animal will serve as a sign.

·מכלל דברייתא בפתוח…QuestionWestwood int. · Jul 29, 2013 · 48:23
Gemara דף כג: מכלל
① The Gemara resolved the apparent contradiction between:
Ⓐ The Braisa, which says that the finder may keep barrels of wine and oil that he found.
Ⓑ and the Mishnah that says that the finder must announce that.
By saying that the Mishnah is talking about resealed barrels.
② the Gemara now asks:
This implies that the Braisa is talking about barrels that were left open.
③ but if so, it is obvious that the finder may keep them.
④ Leaving open barrels leads to the ruining of the contents inside because of bug, snake, contamination, and so on.
⑤ And if so, it would come out that the Braisa is not teaching us anything new.

Key takeaway

By saying that the Mishnah is talking about resealed barrels. This implies that the Braisa is talking about barrels that were left open.

·חזייה דהוה קא מחסם…StatementWestwood int. · Oct 23, 2013 · 37:16
① The Gemara now brings an incident involving Rav pertaining to the matter of whether the place where an object is found is a valid sign or not.
② There was a certain man who found pitch in a wine press.
③ The man came before Rav to determine the status of the found pitch regarding the halacha of returning lost objects.
④ Rav ruled that the man could keep the pitch.
⑤ Rav saw that the man was hesitating to take it.
⑥ Rav told him: if you are afraid to take it, I am telling you that you can divide it with my son Chiya.
⑦ On this incident, the Gemara observes:
Shall we say that Rav holds that the place cannot serve as a sign?
⑧ If place would be a sign, Rav should have told the man to announce the found object. Since it is unusual to find pitch in a winepress.
9. Rabbi Abba answered:
Really, the place is a sign.
10. The circumstance behind the case of Rav was that he saw that weeds were growing out of the pitch.
11. Rav understood that the pitch had been sitting for a long time before it was found.
12. Therefore, perhaps place is a sign
13. But here the owner had already given up hope before the finder found it.
14. Hence, the ruling of Rav that the finder may keep it.

The circumstance behind the case of Rav was that he saw that weeds were growing out of the pitch. Rav understood that the pitch had been sitting for a long time before it was found.

lessons.expl:
·AnswerWestwood int. · Dec 25, 2013 · 36:41
① The Gemara answers: Really? Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is talking about finding? A brand new vessel without a sign.
② In response to the question: If there is no sign, the finder should be permitted to keep it, even if it is not brand new.
③ Regarding this, the Gemara answers:
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is teaching the ruling regarding returning a lost object to a Talmid Chacham.
④ A Talmid Chacham may be shown the object he is coming to claim so that he should try and determine whether or not the lost object is his, based on his sight recognition.
⑤ It is regarding this ruling, that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar comes to clarify and say:
Ⅰ If the object has no sign, but it is not brand new:
Ⓐ The Talmid Chacham might be familiar with this lost object.
Ⓑ If he is shown the object and he says it is his.
Ⓒ The finder should return it to him.
Ⅱ If the object has no sign, and it is brand new:
Ⓐ The Talmid Chacham would not be familiar enough with his lost object.
Ⓑ Therefore, the finder is not obligated to return the lost object to the Talmid Chacham.

① Rashi explained that this refers to a case where the talmid chacham was asked if he was together with his wife.
② And even if it happened to be that he was,
③ Still, he should answer that he was not.
④ Since this is a measure of modesty.
⑤ Tosfos says: it is highly unlikely that a person would be asked such a question. Tosfos gives two other explanations. To explain what is meant by being asked about the bed.
Ⅰ Explanation number one:
Ⓐ A person had an emission, and as a result, he did not come to the beis midrash to study Torah.
Ⓑ When asked upon his return why he did not come to study, he should not say that he had an emission.
Ⓒ but rather:
ⓐ Because he was sick.
ⓑ or some other event. That could prevent a person from attending the Bais HaMidrash.
Ⅱ Explanation number 2:
Ⓐ The Talmid Chacham was asked:
Did you sleep on this bed?
Ⓑ Even if he did, he should say that he did not.
Ⓒ Lest signs of an emission will be seen on the bed.
Ⓓ And this could lead to degrading him.
